analysis.one_liner: Bars children under 14 from farm work and raises penalties for child labor violations.
analysis.headline: The bill raised the minimum age for farm work to 14, boosted civil fines to as much as $50,000 per violation, and added criminal penalties for violations causing a child's death — but it never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The CARE Act would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to close the agricultural exceptions that let children work at younger ages, for longer hours, and in more hazardous conditions than children in any other industry. It would prohibit employment of children under 14 on any farm (except a parent's own farm), ban anyone under 18 from handling pesticides, require employers to report serious injuries, illnesses, and deaths of farm workers under 18 within five days, and raise civil penalties to $15,000–$50,000 per serious-violation, with prison time up to five years for repeated violations causing a child's death or serious injury. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Children working in agriculture, most of them in low-income immigrant families. The bill's own findings note child farmworkers suffer work-related fatalities at over four times the rate of other young workers, and that the exceptions are seldom enforced. It would also protect non-agricultural child workers by raising penalties for child labor violations generally.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employment of children under 14, closing the loophole that lets young children work legally in agriculture while being barred from most other jobs.
Bans anyone under 18 from working as a pesticide handler, a job the bill declares particularly hazardous.

Raises civil penalties for child labor violations to at least $500 and up to $15,000 per employee, or $15,000–$50,000 for violations causing serious injury, illness, or death — doubleable for repeat or willful violations.
Adds criminal penalties of up to five years' imprisonment for willful or repeated child labor violations resulting in a death or serious injury of a worker under 18.
Requires employers to report serious injuries, illnesses, and deaths of agricultural workers under 18 to the Labor Department within five days, with fines of $500–$7,000 for failing to report.
Directs the Labor Department to analyze and annually publish data on children under 18 working in agriculture and on their work-related injuries, illnesses, and deaths.

analysis.who_pays: Growers and farm labor contractors who currently rely on young workers, particularly in hand-harvest crops, would face a smaller legal labor pool, new reporting duties, and much larger fines for violations. Their savings from hiring children at subminimum piece rates would end.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agricultural growers and farm labor contractors

drawbacks.text: Opponents and affected growers would argue the bill would cut the legal supply of labor for hand-harvested crops, raising costs for growers — which could mean higher produce prices or fewer opportunities for farm families who currently work alongside their children.

The bill keeps an exemption only for children working on a farm owned by their own parent, a narrow carve-out that would not cover many family arrangements in small-scale farming, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
Stricter age rules could push some child labor underground rather than eliminating it, since enforcement of existing farm labor rules is already weak, as the bill's findings concede.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — fewer children exposed to heavy machinery, pesticides, and heat, and real penalties when employers break the rules — fall on a population that currently has almost no federal protection, at a cost concentrated in an industry that profits from the status quo. The reporting and penalty provisions are narrowly targeted at serious injury and death, so the cost to compliant employers is limited to recordkeeping. The main design risk is enforcement, which this bill addresses only modestly beyond raising fines.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in June 2019, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard introduced the CARE Act on June 20, 2019, with 24 original cosponsors including Reps. DeLauro, McGovern, Schiff, and Bass.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, where no further action was taken.
It attracted 41 Democratic cosponsors in total — all Democrats — and no Republicans, and no action followed in the 116th Congress.

Because the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, the bill died without a vote; the child labor exceptions it targeted — allowing children to work in agriculture at younger ages and in more hazardous conditions than elsewhere — remained in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Growers and farm labor contractors that depend on child labor, and employers generally who face the same low child-labor penalties as before. Children working in agriculture gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Growers who rely on young farm labor

for.name: Lucille Roybal-Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise farm work minimum ages, ban under-18 pesticide handling, and increase child labor penalties.

for.name: 41 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it all-Democratic support but not enough to move it out of committee.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Bobby Scott, D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 20, 2019 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows the split.

industries.industry: Agricultural growers and farm labor contractors
industries.note: The bill would end the legal employment of children under 14 and bar under-18s from pesticide handling, shrinking the pool of low-wage labor growers currently use for hand harvest, and raise fines for violations from a few thousand to as much as $50,000 per violation. Its interest in keeping the current exceptions runs against the safety of the children doing the work.

industries.industry: U.S. food production and produce supply chains
industries.note: Retail food and produce buyers benefit from inexpensive hand-harvested crops that child labor keeps cheap; the bill would raise harvest costs, which could show up in produce prices, while removing child safety hazards from the supply chain.
